newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FEATURE - Venezuela electric power sector in crisis.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Venezuela electric power sector in crisis.

text.p: Venezuela's electric system, despite an ambitious hydroelectric programme which could soon mean exporting power to neighbours, is on the verge of collapse with industry officials forecasting rationing and even blackouts.
"It's worse than ironic -- it's tragic," said one industry insider who asked not to be named.

While state-owned Electrificacion del Caroni CA (Edelca), which already generates more than 70 percent of the country's power, plans to nearly double its installed generating capacity to over 17,000 megawatts (MW) during the next decade, electricity distribution companies are in a state of anarchy and decay.

"It's a system that is stretched to its limit -- held together with Scotch tape and baling wire, one might say," wrote Robert Bottome, head of local consultants VenEconomy. "It's an accident waiting to happen."
GOVERNMENT RECOGNISES GRAVITY OF SITUATION
Even the government agrees that the situation is dire.

Cadafe, the state-owned electricity holding company which distributes 60 percent of Venezuela's energy, was described recently by Energy and Mines Minister Erwin Arrieta as "torn apart, ruined, broken".

Venezuela boasts one of the region's highest electricity consumption rates. It stood at 2,464 kWh per capita in 1994. In the humid western city of Maracaibo, the second largest in the country, cheap electricity means residents have grown accustomed to low-roofed houses and apartments with air conditioning instead of the airy colonial style houses better suited to the climate.

"Venezuelans have never had to factor electricity into their budgets until now," said the industry expert. But with electricity demand expanding at a five to six percent a year, investment is urgently required.
The industry's chamber, Caveinel, estimates that more than $3 billion needs to be invested over the next three years to repair and maintain the electricity network.
But distorted and erratic rate increases and the failure of public sector clients to pay their bills have left distribution companies with little margin for manoeuvre.
UTILITIES SLAM SLOW RATE APPROVAL

The issue of rates has become a bone of contention in recent months. Caveinel estimated earlier this year that delays in approving rate rises cost the sector more than $150 million in lost revenue between January and May.

Non-payment by the public sector -- a practice which was defended last year by the Attorney General who warned electric companies against cutting off government departments -- cost the sector another $450 million over the same period.

Electricidad de Caracas, the main power supplier to the capital and the largest of Venezuela's six private electric utilities, reported losses and suspended dividends to shareholders. Investment programmes were scaled down.
EDELCA AND CADAFE: MIRROR OPPOSITES IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR
In the public sector, the contrast between Edelca and Cadafe could not be greater.

Edelca has benefited from Venezuela's decision to its exploit hydroelectric potential. With rare foresight, Venezuela eschewed the fact that it controlled the largest proven oil reserves outside the Middle East to embark on an ambitious hydroelectric development along the River Caroni, an Orinoco river tributary.
"Venezuela has an enormous hydroelectric potential on the Caroni," Edelca press chief William Riera Orta told Reuters.

The jewel in the crown in Edelca's hydroelectric programme, the Guri Dam, was completed in 1986. With 20 turbines and capacity of 10,000 MW, it is the second largest hydroelectric generator in the world after the Itaipu dam in Brazil.

In addition to Guri, 60 miles (100 km) upstream of the Caroni's confluence with the Orinoco, Edelca added six turbines and 370 MW at Macagua 55 miles (90 km) downstream. Phase two of the Macagua project should be completed by October next year bringing 14 more turbines and 2,540 MW on line.
A consortium to build another $2 billion, 2,160 MW-capacity project at Caruachi, 40 miles (65 km) below Guri, will be selected early next year.

With its cheap, reliable power, Edelca has been a strong factor in maintaining the widescale development of heavy industry in southeastern Venezuela. It began tentative sales of electricity to neighbouring Colombia in 1992 and there is strong talk of a link to the potentially huge market in northeastern Brazil.
"Edelca has maintained a high degree of professionalism and continuity," said the industry expert.

Cadafe, on the other hand, has suffered from decades of corruption and neglect. Payrolls ballooned as successive governments placed party supporters in control. "It has been used as a political plaything," said the industry insider.
According to one well-placed source, Cadafe's administration does not bill for 38 percent of the power it generates or buys from Edelca. "The system has totally collapsed," the source said.
Cadafe's debts, to suppliers, Paris Club creditors and the Finance Ministry, total more than $1.5 billion.
THE PROMISE OF PRIVATISATION
Privatisation appears to be the only solution. Government officials have been saying for years that this will be the year of the great electric sector sell-off.
But while Edelca is considered a national treasure and never to be privatised, the rest of the state electric sector is clearly not in suitable condition for sale.
An attempt to sell Planta Centro, Latin America's largest thermo-electric generating plant, was aborted in May 1995 after potential bidders demanded clear ground rules for the sector.
Despite recruiting the World Bank's International Finance Corporation (IFC) to advise on privatising the sector over a year ago, little or no progress has been made.
The ground rules, which must include a more efficient rate approval process which redresses the imbalance between industrial and residential rates, have still not been defined.
Arrieta presented a regulatory framework for the sector at a recent cabinet meeting, but its details have not been made public.
First on the privatisation block is due to be the power system on Margarita Island, 20 miles (32 km) off Venezuela's northeast coast.
Now a major Caribbean tourist destination, Margarita has seen electricity demand double since 1987 and the installed capacity of 257 MW has already experienced some shortages.
The sale of Margarita's electric system would be followed by that of Enelven, which supplies power to Maracaibo, and Enelbar which serves the country's fourth city, Barquisimeto.
But the chaotic patterns of debt, confused and inefficient rate structures and decaying infrastructure mean these privatisation plans have stayed firmly on the back-burner.
Meanwhile, as Bottome writes, an attitude of :"We are going to be privatised tomorrow, so why not let the new owner pay for repairs?" leaves the sector in a status quo.
The problem, Bottome adds, is that: "Tomorrow never really comes."
